description_full: John B. Sanfilippo & Son, Inc., through its subsidiary, JBSS Ventures, LLC, engages in the process and distribution of tree nuts and peanuts in the United States. The company offers raw and processed nuts, including almonds, pecans, peanuts, walnuts, cashews, macadamia nuts, pistachios, pine nuts, and filberts in various styles and seasonings; and bar product line, including chewy granola, fruit and grain, sweet and salty, dipped chewy granola, crunchy, energy, fiber, nut, fig, and protein bars. It also offers peanut butter in various sizes and varieties; salad toppings, dried fruit and chocolate, and yogurt coated products; recipe ingredients; bulk food products; sunflower kernels, pepitas, snack mixes, almond and cashew butter, candy and confections, corn snacks, chickpea snacks, sesame sticks, and other sesame snack; and various toppings for ice cream and yogurt. In addition, the company operates a retail store. The company provides its products under the Fisher, Orchard Valley Harvest, Squirrel Brand, and Southern Style Nuts brands as well as under various private brands. It serves retailers and wholesalers, and commercial ingredient and contract packaging customers through a network of independent brokers, distributors, and suppliers. John B. Sanfilippo & Son, Inc. was founded in 1922 and is headquartered in Elgin, Illinois.

financial_summary: John B. Sanfilippo & Son, Inc. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $691M market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 20% against a 7% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $36M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.00× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 37× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 6.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.94x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 36% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.48, it is more defensive than the market.
About $8.8M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 24% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $50.73 (margin of safety -16%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 45%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $37.26 to $71.38 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 12.4 vs 18.3 and EV/EBITDA 7.6 vs 10.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 25% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $94.00 on average, 59% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 7.2% by 13pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.31).
It runs a 18% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.00x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1M of cash against $43.8M of debt), with interest covered 36.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.6% over 3 years, 6.5% over 5 years and 2.1% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 76% of profits supports about 15.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -14.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 3.1x depreciation (7.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 7.6% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and institutions hold 100%.
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 3 sales over the past year, net $1.2M sold.
It returns 6.8% a year to shareholders (1.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, though it has been cut 4.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,770 employees, each generates about $664K of revenue, 1.3x the Consumer Defensive median, and revenue has grown 3.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $20K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
